subsections.subsection_title: What the OSCE station may say

blocks.text: You may encounter these scenarios:
Focused history: A 38-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pressure. Take a focused history and outline your differential diagnoses.
Abdominal examination: Examine a woman with a suspected pelvic mass and report your findings.
Investigation interpretation: Interpret an ultrasound showing multiple uterine fibroids.
Management counselling: Explain the treatment options for symptomatic fibroids.
Fertility counselling: Counsel a woman with fibroids who wishes to conceive.
Acute complication: Assess a pregnant woman with a known fibroid who develops severe abdominal pain.
Preoperative counselling: Explain the benefits and risks of myomectomy versus hysterectomy.
Uterine fibroids, also known as leiomyomas or myomas, are benign tumours arising from the smooth muscle cells of the uterine wall.

They are common during the reproductive years and are influenced by hormonal factors, including oestrogen and progesterone. Their size, number and location determine the symptoms and treatment options.

Fibroids are not cancer, and malignant transformation of a typical fibroid is extremely rare. Leiomyosarcoma is a distinct malignancy that cannot reliably be ruled in or out by simply examining a presumed fibroid.
Located immediately beneath the endometrium and project into the uterine cavity.
Clinical importance: Particularly associated with heavy menstrual bleeding and may impair fertility or increase miscarriage risk, depending on their characteristics.
Located within the myometrium.
Clinical importance: May cause heavy bleeding, uterine enlargement, pelvic pain or pressure, particularly when large or multiple.
Project outward from the external uterine surface.
Clinical importance: More likely to cause pressure symptoms than heavy menstrual bleeding, although symptoms depend on size and location.
Attached to the uterus by a stalk and may project into the cavity or outward from the uterine surface.
Clinical importance: May cause pain if they undergo degeneration or, rarely, torsion.
Fibroids can also be classified using the FIGO leiomyoma classification system, which describes their relationship to the endometrial cavity and uterine serosa.
Fibroids develop through the proliferation of uterine smooth muscle cells and extracellular matrix. Their growth is influenced by reproductive hormones and local growth factors.
Associated factors include:
Increasing reproductive age.
Family history of fibroids.
African ancestry, which is associated with a higher prevalence and, on average, earlier and more symptomatic disease.
Early menarche and other factors associated with lifetime hormonal exposure.
Obesity and certain metabolic factors.

Fibroids commonly shrink after menopause as ovarian hormone levels decline, although postmenopausal bleeding or a growing uterine mass requires appropriate investigation rather than automatic reassurance.
Some women have no symptoms and discover fibroids incidentally during imaging or pregnancy assessment.
This is a common presentation, particularly with submucosal and cavity-distorting fibroids.
Ask about:
Duration of bleeding.
Number of pads used and how often they are changed.
Flooding, leakage or night-time changes.
Passage of clots.
Intermenstrual bleeding.
Fatigue, dizziness, breathlessness or palpitations suggesting anaemia.
Large fibroids may cause:
Pelvic heaviness or abdominal distension.
Urinary frequency or urgency due to bladder compression.
Difficulty emptying the bladder.
Constipation or rectal pressure.
Lower back discomfort.
Pain may occur due to degeneration, pressure, coexisting conditions or, rarely, torsion of a pedunculated fibroid.
Ask whether pain is acute or chronic, whether it relates to menstruation and whether there is fever or pregnancy.
Fibroids may affect fertility, implantation or pregnancy outcomes, particularly when they distort the uterine cavity. However, many women with fibroids conceive and have uncomplicated pregnancies.

Possible pregnancy-related complications include pain from red degeneration, malpresentation, preterm birth, placental complications and postpartum haemorrhage. Risk varies with fibroid size, location and other obstetric factors.

“Good morning. My name is … I understand you have been experiencing symptoms that may be related to your womb. I would like to ask about your menstrual periods, pain, urinary and bowel symptoms, reproductive history and general health. I will then explain the possible causes and investigations. Is that alright?”
Confirm identity, ensure privacy, obtain consent and offer a chaperone if an intimate examination may be required.
Establish the main symptom:
Heavy menstrual bleeding.
Abdominal swelling or pelvic mass.
Pelvic pain.
Urinary or bowel symptoms.
Infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss.
Incidental fibroids detected on ultrasound.
Ask when the symptoms started, how they have progressed and how much they affect daily life.
Ask about:
Age at menarche.
Last menstrual period.
Cycle regularity and frequency.
Duration and amount of bleeding.
Passage of clots and flooding.
Intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.
Dysmenorrhoea.
Previous treatment for heavy bleeding.
Example questions:

items: “How many days does your period usually last?”
“How often do you need to change your sanitary pad?”
“Do you ever soak through your clothes or bedding?”
“Have you experienced dizziness, fainting or unusual tiredness?”

blocks.text: Heavy bleeding is not specific to fibroids. Consider pregnancy-related causes, adenomyosis, endometrial pathology and other causes of abnormal uterine bleeding.
Use SOCRATES:
S — Site: Is the pain suprapubic, generalized or in one side of the pelvis?
O — Onset: Sudden or gradual?
C — Character: Cramping, aching, sharp or pressure-like?
R — Radiation: Does it spread to the back or thighs?
A — Associated symptoms: Fever, vomiting, bleeding or urinary symptoms?
T — Timing: Constant, cyclical or intermittent?
E — Exacerbating/relieving factors: Movement, menstruation, analgesia?
S — Severity: Rate it from 0 to 10.
Sudden severe pain, especially with vomiting, pregnancy or fever, warrants prompt assessment for acute complications and alternative diagnoses.
Ask specifically about:
Frequency and urgency.
Nocturia.
Difficulty starting urination.
Incomplete emptying or retention.
Constipation.
Rectal pressure.
Difficulty passing stool.
Increasing abdominal girth.
A sensation of heaviness.
Difficulty wearing previously comfortable clothing.
Ask about:
Gravidity and parity.
Previous deliveries and mode of delivery.
Miscarriages or ectopic pregnancies.
Duration of attempts to conceive.
Previous fertility investigations or treatment.
Previous caesarean section or other uterine surgery.
Future pregnancy plans.

Clarify that fibroids do not automatically cause infertility. The relationship depends particularly on whether the uterine cavity is distorted, along with the patient's age and other fertility factors.
Ask about:
Previous diagnosis of fibroids.
Previous pelvic ultrasound and whether the fibroids have grown.
Previous myomectomy, hysteroscopy or other uterine procedures.
Endometriosis or adenomyosis.
Contraceptive use.
Cervical screening history, where relevant.
Ask about fatigue, dizziness, palpitations, breathlessness and syncope.
Also ask about:
Bleeding disorders.
Anticoagulant use.
Hypertension and other chronic illnesses.
Previous blood transfusion.
Medications and allergies.
Family history of fibroids or gynaecological disease.
Ask:
“Would you like to preserve your womb even if you do not plan another pregnancy?”
“Would you prefer medication or are you interested in a procedure?”
“How are these symptoms affecting your work and quality of life?”
These questions help guide treatment selection and are frequently rewarded in counselling stations.
Explain the purpose and steps of the examination.
Obtain consent and offer a chaperone.
Ask the patient to empty her bladder if appropriate.
Ensure adequate exposure, privacy and comfort.
Assess vital signs before proceeding if she is actively bleeding or acutely unwell.
Look for:
Pallor, suggesting anaemia.
Tachycardia or hypotension if significant blood loss is suspected.
Signs of haemodynamic compromise.
General distress or pain.
Example report:

“The patient is alert and cooperative. She appears mildly pale but is not in respiratory distress. I would check her vital signs and full blood count because of the history of heavy menstrual bleeding.”
Look for:
Abdominal distension.
Visible lower abdominal mass.
Previous surgical scars.
Visible movement or other abnormalities, if present.
Assess for:
A suprapubic mass arising from the pelvis.
Size, shape, surface and consistency.
Tenderness.
Mobility.
Whether the lower border can be palpated.
Relationship to the pelvis.
A large fibroid uterus may feel firm, irregular and mobile, and may extend above the symphysis pubis. However, examination findings vary.
Perform these when clinically indicated. Percussion may help assess abdominal distension or distinguish a mass from bowel gas, but it does not establish the diagnosis.
Perform when indicated, with consent and a chaperone.
Assess for:
The source of bleeding.
Cervical lesions or abnormalities.
Vaginal or cervical pathology.
Other causes of abnormal bleeding.
Assess:
Uterine size and contour.
Uterine mobility.
Tenderness.
Cervical motion tenderness.
Adnexal masses or tenderness.
Typical findings may include an enlarged, firm uterus with an irregular contour. Submucosal fibroids may produce heavy bleeding without marked uterine enlargement.

content_groups.group_title: E. Examples of abnormal examination reporting

blocks.text: “Abdominal examination reveals a firm, irregular, non-tender suprapubic mass arising from the pelvis. On bimanual examination, the uterus is enlarged and irregular in contour. These findings are suggestive of uterine fibroids. I would arrange pelvic ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis, determine the number and location of fibroids, and assess the need for treatment.”

“There is a firm pelvic mass extending above the symphysis pubis. The mass is relatively mobile and its lower border is not readily palpable abdominally. A uterine origin is suspected, although ovarian and other pelvic masses remain in the differential diagnosis. I would request pelvic imaging.”

items: Example 3 — Fibroids with heavy bleeding and anaemia

blocks.text: “The patient appears pale and has a history of prolonged heavy menstrual bleeding. Abdominal examination demonstrates an enlarged, irregular uterus. My provisional diagnosis is symptomatic uterine fibroids with possible iron-deficiency anaemia. I would assess vital signs, obtain a full blood count and ferritin where appropriate, and arrange pelvic imaging.”

“The patient has marked lower abdominal tenderness in the context of known fibroids. Because acute tenderness is not sufficient to establish fibroid degeneration, I would assess vital signs, exclude pregnancy and urgently investigate other causes of acute pelvic pain.”

“Abdominal and pelvic examinations do not reveal a significant uterine enlargement or palpable mass. This does not exclude smaller or submucosal fibroids. I would correlate the history with pelvic ultrasound and investigate other causes of abnormal uterine bleeding.”

rows: Heavy, painful periods; bulky, globular and often tender uterus
Positive pregnancy test; uterine enlargement may be present
Adnexal mass, sometimes separate from the uterus
Dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel symptoms or infertility
Intermenstrual bleeding or a focal intracavitary lesion
Persistent abnormal bleeding, particularly with relevant risk factors
Fever, discharge, cervical motion tenderness or pelvic tenderness
Concerning clinical or imaging features; cannot be excluded by growth alone

blocks.text: The aim is to confirm the presence and location of fibroids, assess their impact and exclude other causes of symptoms.
Perform urine or serum β-hCG when pregnancy is possible, particularly with amenorrhoea, pelvic pain or abnormal bleeding.
Assess haemoglobin and red-cell indices in patients with heavy menstrual bleeding or symptoms of anaemia.
Ferritin may be useful if iron deficiency is suspected. Treat confirmed iron deficiency as appropriate.
Ultrasound is usually the first-line imaging investigation.
It can assess:
Uterine size and contour.
Number and dimensions of fibroids.
Location and relationship to the endometrial cavity.
Ovaries and adnexa.
Other possible causes of pelvic symptoms.
Example ultrasound report:

“Pelvic ultrasound demonstrates an enlarged uterus containing multiple well-defined solid myometrial lesions consistent with leiomyomas. The largest lesion measures 6 cm and is intramural. The relationship of the lesions to the endometrial cavity should be documented to guide management.”
The FIGO system classifies fibroids according to their relationship to the uterine cavity and serosal surface.

rows: Entirely intramural but contacts the endometrium
Other locations, including cervical or parasitic fibroids

blocks.text: Hybrid fibroids can involve both the endometrial and serosal surfaces and are described using two numbers, such as 2–5.

Exam pearl: The location matters as much as the size. A small submucosal fibroid may cause substantial bleeding and fertility problems, while a larger subserosal fibroid may mainly cause pressure symptoms.
MRI may be useful when:
Ultrasound findings are inconclusive.
There are numerous or very large fibroids.
Detailed mapping is needed before surgery or a procedure.
Adenomyosis or another pelvic condition is also suspected.
MRI is not necessary for every patient.

content_groups.group_title: F. Hysteroscopy or saline infusion sonography

blocks.text: These may be useful when a submucosal fibroid or other intracavitary lesion is suspected and additional cavity assessment would change management.
Depending on symptoms and clinical findings, consider:
Renal function if urinary obstruction is suspected.
Coagulation tests if there is a history suggesting a bleeding disorder.
Cervical assessment or endometrial sampling when indicated by the bleeding pattern, age and risk factors.
Endometrial sampling is not routinely required for every patient with fibroids; it is used when another endometrial cause of abnormal bleeding needs investigation.
Management depends on symptoms, fibroid size and location, anaemia, age, reproductive plans, comorbidities and patient preference.
An asymptomatic fibroid does not automatically require treatment.
Assess the severity of bleeding and pain.
Check haemodynamic stability if bleeding is heavy.
Assess for anaemia and treat iron deficiency.
Confirm the diagnosis and map the fibroids with imaging.
Ask about future pregnancy and uterine-preservation preferences.
Discuss conservative, medical, procedural and surgical options.
If the patient is haemodynamically unstable from acute bleeding, urgent stabilization and specialist management take priority over routine outpatient treatment.
Suitable for selected patients who have no symptoms or mild symptoms that do not affect quality of life.
Management may include:
Explanation and reassurance.
Review if symptoms develop or worsen.
Repeat imaging when clinically indicated, rather than automatically scanning every patient at fixed intervals.
Reduces menstrual blood loss and is taken during menstruation when prescribed. It does not shrink fibroids. Assess thrombotic history and contraindications.
Examples include ibuprofen or naproxen. They can relieve menstrual pain and may reduce bleeding. Consider gastrointestinal, renal and other contraindications.

Combined hormonal contraception or a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system may reduce bleeding in suitable patients. An LNG-IUS may be unsuitable if the uterine cavity is significantly distorted.

Oral iron is commonly used for iron deficiency; intravenous iron may be appropriate when oral treatment is unsuitable, ineffective or rapid correction is required. Iron treats the deficiency, not the fibroids themselves.

GnRH agonists or antagonists: Can reduce bleeding and, depending on the preparation, reduce fibroid volume. Hypoestrogenic effects, bone health, duration of treatment and add-back therapy require consideration.
Short-term preoperative treatment: May improve haemoglobin and reduce fibroid size in selected patients before surgery.

Selective progesterone receptor modulators: Availability and regulatory status vary; ulipristal acetate has important liver-safety restrictions in some jurisdictions and should not be treated as a routine first-line option.
Medical treatment often controls symptoms rather than permanently eliminating fibroids. Symptoms may recur when treatment is stopped.
Removes suitable submucosal fibroids through the cervix using a hysteroscope. It may improve heavy bleeding and can be helpful when a cavity-distorting fibroid is associated with infertility.

Removes fibroids while preserving the uterus. It may be performed hysteroscopically, laparoscopically or by open surgery, depending on size, number, location and available expertise. Recurrence is possible.

Blocks blood supply to fibroids to reduce their size and symptoms. It avoids major uterine surgery in many cases, but reproductive outcomes and pregnancy risks require careful discussion when future pregnancy is desired.
Definitive treatment for uterine fibroids when the uterus is removed. It is an option for severe symptoms when fertility is no longer desired and other treatments are unsuitable or unwanted.
Other selected options include MRI-guided focused ultrasound or radiofrequency ablation where available and clinically appropriate.
This is a frequent counselling question.

rows: New or residual fibroids may develop
Uterine fibroids cannot recur after complete removal of the uterus
Complexity depends on fibroid number, size and location
Complexity depends on uterine size, surgical route and other factors

blocks.text: Myomectomy can involve significant blood loss and may lead to adhesions or uterine scarring. Some patients who have a myomectomy may require planned caesarean delivery in a future pregnancy, depending on the depth and location of uterine incisions.

Hysterectomy involves operative risks such as bleeding, infection, injury to surrounding organs and venous thromboembolism. Ovarian removal is not automatically required when hysterectomy is performed for fibroids.

content_groups.group_title: F. Which treatment should you choose?

items: Reassurance, observation and review if symptoms change
Treat anaemia and offer suitable medical treatment
Persistent symptoms, pressure or fertility concerns
Consider location-specific procedures, myomectomy, UAE or other specialist options
Severe symptoms; fertility no longer desired

blocks.text: This is a general decision framework. The actual choice depends on clinical findings, contraindications, availability and patient preference.
A woman with fibroids who wishes to conceive needs individualized assessment.
Discuss the following:
Submucosal fibroids: Those that distort the uterine cavity are particularly relevant to implantation and fertility; removal may be considered.

Intramural fibroids: Their effect depends on size, number and proximity to or distortion of the endometrial cavity. Evidence does not support removing every intramural fibroid simply because a patient is infertile.
Subserosal fibroids: Usually have less direct impact on fertility unless they cause other problems.
Other infertility factors: Assess age, ovulation, tubal patency and semen parameters where indicated.
Surgical risks: Myomectomy may improve outcomes in selected cases but can cause adhesions, bleeding and uterine scarring.
Pregnancy after surgery: The interval before attempting conception and the mode of delivery should be individualized by the treating specialist.
Model counselling statement:

“Fibroids are common benign growths of the womb, and many women with fibroids become pregnant. The effect on fertility depends largely on their location and whether they distort the cavity where a pregnancy implants. We would review your scan and assess other fertility factors before recommending surgery. Removing fibroids may help in selected cases, but it also has risks, so the decision should be based on your individual circumstances.”

content_groups.group_title: A. Heavy bleeding with haemodynamic compromise

blocks.text: Look for:
Tachycardia.
Hypotension.
Syncope or confusion.
Marked pallor.
Ongoing heavy bleeding.
Management begins with urgent assessment, stabilization, appropriate blood tests and crossmatching when indicated, and specialist involvement. Do not delay resuscitation while waiting for imaging.
Red degeneration is haemorrhagic infarction of a fibroid and is particularly associated with pregnancy.
Features may include:
Acute localized abdominal pain.
Tenderness over the fibroid.
Occasionally nausea or low-grade fever.
Known fibroids on prior imaging.

It is a diagnosis made after considering other important causes of pain. Management is often conservative with appropriate analgesia and obstetric or gynaecological review, depending on pregnancy status and clinical severity.

content_groups.group_title: C. Torsion of a pedunculated fibroid

blocks.text: This is uncommon but can cause sudden severe pain and may require urgent surgical assessment.
A large fibroid may compress the urinary tract. Difficulty passing urine, retention, hydronephrosis or impaired renal function requires prompt assessment and management.
Fibroids may be associated with pain, malpresentation, preterm birth and postpartum haemorrhage. Management depends on gestation, fibroid location, symptoms and obstetric findings.

subsections.subsection_title: Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What are uterine fibroids?
Benign tumours arising from the smooth muscle of the uterus, also known as leiomyomas.
Q2. What are the main types of fibroids?
Submucosal, intramural and subserosal fibroids. Pedunculated fibroids are attached by a stalk and may be intracavitary or external to the uterus.
Q3. What is the commonest symptom?
Heavy menstrual bleeding is a common presentation. Other symptoms include pelvic pressure, abdominal enlargement, pain, urinary symptoms and fertility difficulties. Some patients are asymptomatic.
Q4. What are the typical examination findings?
An enlarged, firm, irregularly contoured pelvic mass that appears to arise from the uterus. Examination may be normal in smaller fibroids.
Q5. What is the first-line investigation?
Pelvic ultrasound, usually transvaginal when appropriate, to determine the size, number and location of fibroids.
Q6. Which fibroids are most associated with fertility problems?
Submucosal and other cavity-distorting fibroids are particularly relevant. The significance of intramural fibroids depends on their characteristics and the individual fertility assessment.
Q7. What is the difference between myomectomy and hysterectomy?
Myomectomy removes fibroids while preserving the uterus. Hysterectomy removes the uterus and is definitive treatment for uterine fibroids, but eliminates the ability to carry a pregnancy.
Q8. What is uterine artery embolization?
A minimally invasive procedure that blocks blood supply to fibroids, causing them to shrink and symptoms to improve. Future pregnancy plans require careful discussion before choosing this option.
Q9. Do all fibroids require surgery?
No. Asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic fibroids can often be observed. Medical treatment, procedures or surgery are selected according to symptoms, anatomy and patient preferences.
Q10. What is red degeneration?
Haemorrhagic infarction of a fibroid, often associated with pregnancy, causing acute localized pain and tenderness. Other urgent causes of abdominal pain must be excluded.
Q11. Can fibroids cause anaemia?
Yes. Heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding may lead to iron-deficiency anaemia.
Q12. Do fibroids always shrink after menopause?
They often shrink because of declining ovarian hormone levels, but this is not guaranteed. Postmenopausal bleeding or a concerning mass requires evaluation.
Q13. Can fibroids become cancerous?

Typical fibroids are benign. Leiomyosarcoma is a distinct malignancy; it is not generally understood to arise through routine malignant transformation of an ordinary fibroid. Concerning symptoms or imaging findings warrant appropriate specialist assessment.
Q14. When would you consider hysterectomy?
For severe or persistent symptoms when other treatments are unsuitable, ineffective or unwanted, particularly when the patient does not desire future pregnancy and understands the implications.
Assuming that every pelvic mass is a fibroid without excluding pregnancy or an adnexal mass.
Forgetting to assess haemodynamic stability in a patient with severe bleeding.
Failing to assess anaemia.
Assuming that fibroid size alone determines symptom severity.
Failing to document the location of fibroids on ultrasound.
Recommending myomectomy without discussing recurrence, bleeding and adhesions.
Recommending hysterectomy without confirming reproductive wishes and obtaining informed consent.
Assuming that every fibroid causes infertility.
Missing urinary obstruction or acute complications.
Treating fibroids in pregnancy without excluding other causes of abdominal pain.
